title: The Basic Git-to-Deploy Flow
intro: Almost every CI/CD pipeline starts the same way: branch, commit, push, let automation take over. Let's walk the flow.

steps.prompt: Create and switch to a new branch called 'fix-login-bug'.
steps.explanation: Branching keeps your change isolated from main until it's reviewed and merged.
steps.why: 'git checkout -b' combines creating the branch and switching to it in one step — the equivalent two-step form is 'git branch fix-login-bug' followed by 'git checkout fix-login-bug', which is just more typing for the same result.

steps.prompt: Stage and commit your changes with the message 'fix: handle expired session tokens'.
expected_commands: git add . && git commit -m "fix: handle expired session tokens"
git commit -am "fix: handle expired session tokens"
steps.fake_output:
[fix-login-bug a1b2c3d] fix: handle expired session tokens
 1 file changed, 12 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)
steps.explanation: Descriptive, conventional commit messages (fix:, feat:, chore:) often drive automated changelogs and versioning in real pipelines.
steps.why: 'commit -am' only stages files that are already tracked by git — a genuinely new file still needs an explicit 'git add' first. 'add . && commit -m' is the safer habit when you're not sure whether everything changed is already tracked.

steps.explanation: This alone often triggers a CI workflow (on: push in GitHub Actions) that runs tests automatically.
steps.why: Without specifying 'origin fix-login-bug' the first time you push a new branch, plain 'git push' fails asking you to set an upstream — this explicit form sets it up in the same command instead of needing a follow-up.

steps.prompt: Open a pull request from this branch into main using the GitHub CLI.
steps.fake_output:
? Title: fix: handle expired session tokens
Creating pull request for fix-login-bug into main
https://github.com/you/repo/pull/42
steps.explanation: PR creation itself often triggers a separate CI workflow (on: pull_request) — commonly a stricter set of checks than plain push.
steps.why: You could open the PR through the GitHub web UI instead — 'gh pr create' exists specifically so this whole flow (branch, commit, push, PR) never requires leaving the terminal, which matters when you're doing it dozens of times a week.

steps.prompt: Check the status of the CI run on this PR.
steps.explanation: Lint failed but build/test passed — worth knowing at a glance which specific job to look at rather than treating the whole pipeline as one blob.
steps.why: 'gh pr view' scopes the check list to this one PR specifically; 'gh run list' shows every recent workflow run across the whole repo — reach for pr view when you already know which PR you care about, run list when you're scanning broadly.

steps.prompt: View the failed run's logs to see what lint caught.
steps.fake_output: src/auth.js:34:5 error 'unusedVar' is defined but never used
steps.explanation: --log-failed filters straight to the failing job's output instead of dumping the entire pipeline log.
steps.why: Without --log-failed, 'gh run view --log' dumps every job's full output including the ones that already passed — for a pipeline with several jobs, that's a lot of scrolling to find the one line that actually matters.
